raw_case_text:
A 12-year-old Indian boy was admitted to our institution with a prolonged fever of 1 month duration, with maximum temperatures above 40 C. This was associated with watery, nonbloody diarrhea, with intermittent vomiting and abdominal pain. There was a travel history to India for 1 month, and the patient had returned to Singapore 1 week prior to the admission. The patient had visited several rural areas in Kerala and Bangalore during his travel. There was no history of raw food intake or animal contact. His vaccinations were up-to-date according to the national immunization schedule, but he had not received the typhoid vaccine prior to travel. At this time, his 21-year-old older sister was also admitted to another hospital with fever and diarrhea. There was no prior treatment with antibiotics. No significant past illnesses were reported.
On admission, the child was alert and oriented and no pallor or jaundice was noted. Mucosal membranes appeared dry but perfusion was good with a capillary-refill time of less than 2 seconds. His temperature was 38.2 C, with a pulse rate of 150 bpm and a blood pressure of 90/48 mm Hg. On examination, his heart sounds were dual and breath sounds were vesicular, with no added sounds. His abdomen was soft, with mild tenderness over the right hypochondrium, and there was no guarding or rigidity. He had no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. There was no rash or eschar noted. The rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable. Heart rate and blood pressure responded well to a fluid bolus given in the emergency department and subsequently remained stable. He was started empirically on intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day for presumptive enteric fever.
The aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures grew Salmonella typhi, which were sensitive to ampicillin, co-trimoxazole and ceftriaxone. Widal Weil Felix (WWF) serology showed titers of 1/160 for S typhi O-AB, 1/640 for S typhi H-AB, 1/80 for Salmonella paratyphi A O-AB, 1/320 for S paratyphi A H-AB, and 1/80 for S paratyphi B O-AB. Proteus OXK AB and Proteus OX19 AB were not detected. The full blood count showed pancytopenia, with a hemoglobin level of 8.7 g/dL, white blood cell count of 3.47 x 109/L and a platelet count of 90 x 109/L. Liver function tests revealed elevated transaminases with an alanine transaminase level of 188 U/L and an aspartate transaminase level of 186 U/L. An ultrasound of the abdomen showed cecal and terminal ileal bowel wall thickening with enlargement of mesenteric lymph nodes.
The patient continued to be persistently febrile despite 9 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. Repeat blood cultures were negative for bacterial growth. Oral co-trimoxazole 4 mg/kg BD was added to provide added cover for typhoid fever. Table 1 shows the timeline of his hematological and biochemical investigations. Microbiological investigations performed are summarized in Table 2.
On day 16 of ceftriaxone and oral co-trimoxazole, the patient remained persistently febrile. Diarrhea was also persistent although noted to be on an improving trend. At this point, a further infective workup was done, which included blood film for malaria parasite, Rickettsia typhi serology and Orientia tsutsugamushi serology. Two days later, Orientia tsutsugamushi serology results returned positive at IgG >=64. The patient was started on oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. Ceftriaxone and co-trimoxazole were stopped. Fever resolved on day 2 of doxycycline, and the patient was discharged after being afebrile for more than 24 hours, to complete a 7-day course of doxycycline. Subsequent follow-up revealed a well child with complete resolution of fever and symptoms.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 12-year-old Indian boy presented with prolonged fever of 1 month duration with temperatures exceeding 40 °C, accompanied by watery diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced prolonged fever for 1 month with maximum temperatures above 40 °C, associated with watery, nonbloody diarrhea, intermittent vomiting, and abdominal pain. His 21-year-old sister was concurrently hospitalized elsewhere with fever and diarrhea. No prior antibiotic therapy had been administered.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past illnesses. Vaccinations were up to date according to national schedule, but had not received travel-specific immunizations prior to departure. Travel history: 1-month travel to rural areas in Kerala and Bangalore, India, returning to Singapore 1 week prior to admission. Denied raw food intake or animal contact.
subjective.review_of_systems: Watery nonbloody diarrhea, intermittent vomiting, and abdominal pain as noted in HPI.

objective.physical_examination: Alert and oriented; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill time <2 seconds; no pallor or jaundice. Temperature: 38.2 °C, pulse rate: 150 bpm, blood pressure: 90/48 mmHg (stabilized after fluid bolus). Cardiovascular: dual heart sounds, no murmurs. Respiratory: vesicular breath sounds without added sounds. Abdomen: soft with mild tenderness over right hypochondrium; no guarding, rigidity, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly. Skin: no rash or eschar noted.
objective.routine_investigations: Full blood count showed pancytopenia: hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 3.47 x 10^9/L, platelet count 90 x 10^9/L. Liver function tests: ALT 188 U/L, AST 186 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound showed cecal and terminal ileal bowel wall thickening with mesenteric lymph node enlargement. Blood film for malaria parasite: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Proteus OXK AB and Proteus OX19 AB were not detected.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Typhoid fever (enteric fever) with concurrent Orientia tsutsugamushi (scrub typhus) coinfection. Aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures grew Salmonella typhi sensitive to ampicillin, co-trimoxazole, and ceftriaxone. Widal Weil Felix serology demonstrated titers of 1/160 for S. typhi O-AB, 1/640 for S. typhi H-AB, 1/80 for Salmonella paratyphi A O-AB, 1/320 for S. paratyphi A H-AB, and 1/80 for S. paratyphi B O-AB. He received empiric IV ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day, with oral co-trimoxazole 4 mg/kg twice daily added on day 9 for persistent fever (repeat blood cultures were negative). Due to fever persistence on day 16, Orientia tsutsugamushi serology was obtained and returned positive (IgG >=64; Rickettsia typhi serology was evaluated). Ceftriaxone and co-trimoxazole were stopped, and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily was initiated. Fever resolved on day 2 of doxycycline, and he completed a 7-day course with complete symptom resolution.
